name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
title: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
answer: Federated sharing of sensitive data refers to systems that let institutions keep sensitive datasets within their own infrastructure while still allowing approved researchers to run analyses across them. It covers clinical records, administrative data, survey responses, and other protected research materials that cannot be copied into a central repository. The goal is to widen access to evidence without moving raw data or exposing identifying details. In research data and repositories, this sits between fully open archives and closed data safe havens.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Federated sharing of sensitive data refers to systems that let institutions keep sensitive datasets within their own infrastructure while still allowing approved researchers to run analyses across them. It covers clinical records, administrative data, survey responses, and other protected research materials that cannot be copied into a central repository. The goal is to widen access to evidence without moving raw data or exposing identifying details. In research data and repositories, this sits between fully open archives and closed data safe havens.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a network of nodes, one at each data holder, connected by a coordination service that sends queries and receives aggregate results. Each node typically includes a secure compute environment, local storage, and an API that enforces the data holder's access rules. The site's catalogue of 801 scientific models and 732 AI tools reflects the range of software components that can be deployed inside such nodes, though the federated layer itself is usually lightweight middleware rather than a single platform.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The dominant approach is to move the analysis to the data, not the data to the analyst. A researcher submits a query or model training job, the coordination layer distributes it to each node, and each node returns only summary statistics, gradients, or model updates. Techniques such as secure aggregation, differential privacy, and synthetic data generation are used to reduce the risk that any returned output reveals an individual record. The site's 10,555 extracted claims from research works document many of these methods as they appear in peer reviewed papers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk are managed through data use agreements, federated identity, and audit logs at each node. The data holder retains control over what queries are permitted, which variables are exposed, and when a result is too disclosive to release. Provenance is recorded at the query level, so a published finding can be traced back to the contributing nodes and the version of each dataset used. Because the site links to original papers rather than a search tool, readers can inspect the governance details reported in each study.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Federated sharing is moving toward more routine use in multi-site clinical and social science research, with standard protocols for query languages and disclosure checks. The main open problems are computational cost, heterogeneity of local data schemas, and the difficulty of proving that a sequence of federated queries cannot be combined to re-identify individuals. As the site's library of 135 research papers grows, it is likely to track how these systems handle real-world sensitive data at scale and how regulators respond to federated evidence.
